teaser.text: Franco-Nevada turns other companies’ mines, wells and commodity interests into long-lived financial assets. It receives money or metal under contracts while leaving operators to run the underlying properties.

blocks.heading: What has to go right—and wrong for Franco-Nevada?

paragraphs.text: The starting point is the US$900.7 million five-year average after adding back the Cobre Panamá impairment. The roughly 2% annual increase follows management’s 2026-to-2030 GEO midpoint outlook. The bear case falls to US$757 million in 2027 and recovers only to US$820 million by 2029 because lower prices, delays and entitlement reductions persist. The bull case reaches US$1,000 million first and US$1,126 million last, requiring stronger deliveries, project ramps and a durable Panama agreement.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Franco-Nevada really make?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow became negative in 2025 because acquisitions cost $2,191.6 million, almost all of the $2,196.7 million capital-spending total. The $1.05 billion Côté transaction illustrates the distinction: Franco-Nevada bought future royalty income from IAMGOLD and Sumitomo’s mine rather than machinery needed to maintain existing operations. Negative free cash flow can therefore signal expansion, not weak contracts.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay today for Franco-Nevada?

paragraphs.text: The valuation therefore demands confidence in both durability and growth. The price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E, shows how much investors pay for each dollar of profit. The forward P/E is lower than the trailing P/E, which means the price assumes earnings will rise. Enterprise value adds the business value after adjusting equity value for financing assets and obligations, so it tests the portfolio and balance sheet together.

dividend.title: Franco-Nevada dividend: payout and coverage
dividend.meta_description: Franco-Nevada's dividend history, cash coverage, future drivers and current yield, explained in plain English.
dividend.opening: Franco-Nevada paid US$1.43 per share in dividends in 2025. Its cash did not cover the full shareholder payout: US$5.07 per share was paid out in excess of free cash flow.
dividend.closing: The full Franco-Nevada memo also covers its business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: How much does Franco-Nevada pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: Revenue rose 63.7% in 2025 as gold prices increased. GEOs Sold remained below 2021–22 levels. Diluted EPS was US$5.76 in 2025. It was US$2.87 in 2024. The key turn is the company’s own free cash flow: 37.4% of revenue in 2024 became -38.9% in 2025 as acquisitions drove spending. The shortfall left US$5.07 per share paid out in excess of free cash flow; dividends were US$1.43 per share. Year-end net cash was US$670.9 million.

blocks.heading: Does Franco-Nevada's cash cover its dividend?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow was US$194.9 million in 2021. It rose to US$858.0 million in 2022, then remained positive at US$469.6 million in 2023 and US$421.5 million in 2024. In 2025 it turned negative at US$703.0 million because this measure deducts purchases of royalty and stream interests. Negative free cash flow therefore meant heavy reinvestment, not that the existing portfolio stopped producing cash.

Shareholders still received rising dividends. Dividends paid increased from US$179.6 million in 2021 to US$275.1 million in 2025, while the company bought back no shares in any of the five years. At year-end, cash and short-term investments stood at US$670.9 million, with no debt. The company had spent its reserve aggressively without creating a lasting borrowing burden.

paragraphs.text: Base dividends begin at US$1.76 per share and reach US$2.08 by 2029. The bear case holds them at US$1.60, while the bull case reaches US$2.76. The base reflects the latest US$0.44 quarterly dividend and a history of annual increases, moderated because acquisitions and weak deliveries can compete for cash.

The bear case would gain weight if gold prices fall, deliveries weaken, or Candelaria and Antapaccay reductions arrive before replacement projects contribute, particularly through the second half of 2027 and 2028. A failure to secure a restart agreement would keep Panama’s receipts finite.

earnings.title: Franco-Nevada earnings: guidance and results
earnings.meta_description: Franco-Nevada reports next on November 11, 2026; see guidance, recent results and whether mine deliveries improve.
earnings.opening: Franco-Nevada's next results are expected on November 11, 2026. The key thing to watch is whether Candelaria, Côté and Tocantinzinho turn expected improvements into receipts while Antamina faces lower Q3 deliveries.
earnings.closing: The full Franco-Nevada memo also answers how Franco-Nevada makes money, who its rivals are, how management is paid, and which risks could change the outlook.

paragraphs.text: GEOs, or gold equivalent ounces, put different metals into one common unit. Management guides to 510,000–570,000 GEOs for 2026. Its 2030 outlook is 555,000–615,000 GEOs without a full Cobre Panamá restart. The guidance depends on improvements at Candelaria, Côté and Tocantinzinho, while Cobre Panamá stockpile deliveries remain finite.

By 2030, management expects 555,000–615,000 GEOs without a full Cobre Panamá restart. That growth must offset contractual reductions: Candelaria’s entitlement is expected to fall from 68% to 40%, while Antapaccay will move to 30% of gold and silver production. The next question is whether analysts think this plan will produce the promised earnings.

blocks.heading: Did Franco-Nevada keep its production promise?

paragraphs.text: Franco-Nevada forecast 465,000–525,000 gold-equivalent ounces for 2025 and delivered 519,106. A gold-equivalent ounce converts different commodity receipts into a common gold measure. Hitting guidance shows portfolio execution, but mine operators control production and commodity prices affect the conversion.

blocks.heading: What have Franco-Nevada's last eight quarters shown?

paragraphs.text: Operating cash improved, while free cash flow swung positive because acquisition spending fell sharply. The eight-quarter record shows how investment timing can change free cash flow even when revenue rises. Antamina’s warning of lower third-quarter deliveries is therefore more useful for forecasting than one unusually strong quarter.

blocks.heading: What should people watch in Franco-Nevada's next results?

paragraphs.text: Candelaria, Côté and Tocantinzinho must turn their expected improvements into Franco-Nevada receipts. Antamina also matters because management expects lower Q3 deliveries after reduced concentrator throughput in Q2. A concentrator separates valuable minerals from mined rock, so lower throughput can reduce later deliveries even after production conditions improve.
